To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
substance abuse is common in cancer patients, is associated with a number of negative consequences, and can be treated effectively.
substance use disorders are common in the cancer population and that the prevalence of substance use disorders increases with the severity of cancer-related symptoms.

(a) the prevalence of substance abuse in patients with cancer appears to be similar to that in the general population, (b) the prevalence of abuse in patients with advanced disease may be as high as 50% to 60% and is likely to be higher than in the general population with the same disease, (c) the prevalence of alcohol abuse is higher than that of drug abuse, (d) the prevalence of drug abuse in the cancer patient is higher for opiates than for other
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and treatment of substance abuse in cancer patients.
the development and evaluation of new methods of treatment of cancer.
the development of an integrated model for the management of the cancer patient with a history of substance-abusing behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a paucity of data to support the notion that cancer patients with a history of addiction have an increased likelihood of aberrant drug behavior during the treatment of their malignancy.
the oncology clinician should be aware of the potential for substance abuse, should be able to recognize it, and should be able to manage it in a safe, humane, and effective manner.
there are no definitive guidelines for the evaluation and management of the cancer patient who abuses alcohol, drugs, or both.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the oncologist should not hesitate to prescribe potentially abusable drugs when they are needed to provide adequate symptom control, and that patients with a history of substance use disorders should not be denied the benefits of such treatment because of their past history.

the use of potentially abusive drugs for symptom control in the cancer population should be considered in the context of the patient's overall clinical status and should not be considered a risk factor for addiction.
we have provided a framework for understanding and addressing the complex relationship between substance abuse and cancer care.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the oncologist should be aware of the potential for aberrant drug-taking behaviors in patients with cancer and should be familiar with the tools available to assess these behaviors and to manage them.
the management of substance abuse and addiction in patients with cancer is a multifaceted process.
patients with a history of addiction should be managed by oncologists with expertise in the field of substance abuse, preferably in collaboration with a multidisciplinary team.
